title: CV & LinkedIn for AI roles
summary: Turn your projects and maths background into a sharp, keyword-aware CV and LinkedIn profile that passes screens and lands AI interviews.
objectives: Structure a one-page CV that an AI recruiter and ATS can both read
Translate your maths degree and support internship into relevant strengths
Write impact bullets using the action-plus-metric formula
Tailor keywords to a job description without keyword stuffing
Optimise a LinkedIn headline, About section, and Featured projects
Link a clean GitHub and portfolio that back up every claim
Avoid the common mistakes that get early-career CVs rejected

quiz.q: What does ATS stand for, and why does it matter for your CV?
quiz.answer: Applicant Tracking System — software that parses and ranks CVs before a human sees them, so layout and keywords must be machine-readable.
quiz.why: Many AI-role applications are filtered by an ATS first; a fancy multi-column or image-based CV can be parsed into garbage and rejected automatically.

quiz.q: Which bullet is strongest on an AI CV?
options: Worked on a machine learning project
Built a churn model in Python with scikit-learn, reaching 0.89 ROC-AUC on held-out data
Responsible for data and modelling tasks
Interested in AI and passionate about data
quiz.why: It names the action, the tools, and a concrete metric — recruiters and hiring managers can instantly judge the impact.

quiz.q: Where should your most important keywords and projects appear?
options: Only in a skills list at the bottom
Near the top, in the summary and first project
Hidden in white text for the ATS
quiz.why: Recruiters skim top-down for seconds; the top third of the CV must carry your headline skills and best project, and hidden white text is a trick that gets you blacklisted.

quiz.q: True or false — you should send the same CV to every AI job.
quiz.why: False. Tailor the summary, skills order, and project emphasis to each job description so the relevant keywords and strengths surface first.

quiz.q: Name two things a strong LinkedIn headline for an aspiring AI engineer should do.
quiz.answer: State the target role or direction (e.g. Aspiring ML Engineer) and signal concrete skills or evidence (Python, building NLP projects) rather than just a job title.
quiz.why: The headline is searchable and is the first thing recruiters see; a specific, skill-rich headline appears in more searches and reads as credible.

quiz.q: Why should every claim on your CV map to something a recruiter can verify?
quiz.answer: Because interviewers probe your CV; a GitHub repo, demo link, or metric you can explain proves the claim and protects you from being caught out.
quiz.why: Unverifiable buzzwords invite tough questions; linked, explainable evidence turns claims into a credible, interview-winning story.

body_markdown:
## Why your CV is a data pipeline

Think of an application like a pipeline. Your CV is the input, an **ATS** (Applicant Tracking System) often parses it first, a recruiter skims it for seconds, and only then does a hiring manager read it carefully. If any stage chokes, you never reach an interview. Your job is to make every stage flow.

As a maths graduate moving into AI, you have a real edge: rigour, probability, linear algebra, and proof-level thinking. The CV's job is to make that edge **obvious and relevant** to an AI role.

## Structure that survives an ATS

Keep it **one page**, single column, plain fonts, real text (never an image of text). A clean order works best:

1. **Name + contact + links** (GitHub, LinkedIn, portfolio).
2. **Summary** — two lines: who you are, your direction, your strongest evidence.
3. **Skills** — grouped: languages, ML/data, tools.
4. **Projects** — your strongest first, with metrics.
5. **Experience** — your L1 support internship, framed for impact.
6. **Education** — your maths degree.

Avoid tables, text boxes, and multi-column layouts — many parsers scramble them.

## Impact bullets: action + tool + metric

Weak bullets describe duties. Strong bullets describe **impact**. Use the formula: *action verb -> what you built -> with which tools -> measurable result*.

```text
Weak:   Worked on a machine learning model for customer data.
Strong: Built a churn classifier in Python (scikit-learn);
        reached 0.89 ROC-AUC and shipped it behind a FastAPI endpoint.
```

Numbers can be model metrics, dataset size, latency, users, or time saved. Even a personal project metric beats a vague verb.

## Tailoring keywords without faking

Read the job description and mirror its real language. If it says "NLP" and "PyTorch", use those exact terms **where they are true**. A quick way to spot overlap is to count which of your skills appear in the posting.

```python
job_desc = open("job.txt").read().lower()
my_skills = ["python", "pytorch", "sql", "nlp", "fastapi", "docker"]
matches = [s for s in my_skills if s in job_desc]
missing = [s for s in my_skills if s not in job_desc]
print("emphasise:", matches)
print("deprioritise:", missing)
```

Lead with the matched skills. Never claim a skill you cannot defend in an interview.

## LinkedIn that recruiters can find

LinkedIn is a search engine. Three fields do the heavy lifting:

- **Headline**: name your target plus concrete skills, e.g. *Aspiring ML Engineer | Python, scikit-learn, NLP | Maths graduate*.
- **About**: a short story — maths foundation, the pivot into AI, two project highlights, what you're looking for.
- **Featured**: pin your best project repo, a demo, or a write-up so claims are clickable.

Fill the Skills section with the exact terms recruiters search, and ask a mentor or peer for one endorsement on each top skill.

## Make every claim verifiable

Interviewers probe what's on the page. Every project should map to a **GitHub repo with a clear README**, ideally a live demo or notebook. Your profile README and pinned repos are part of your CV now.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/you/churn-api
cd churn-api
open README.md   # screenshots, metrics, how to run
```

## Your task

Rewrite your CV to one page with three metric-driven project bullets, then update your LinkedIn headline and Featured section to match.

slides.title: Your CV is a pipeline
bullets: A T S parses it, recruiter skims, manager reads.
Each stage can reject you in seconds.
Maths rigour is your edge — make it relevant.
slides.narration: Think of your application as a data pipeline. Your C V is the input. Very often an applicant tracking system, or A T S, parses it first. Then a recruiter skims it for just a few seconds, and only then does a hiring manager read it properly. If any stage chokes, you never reach an interview. Your maths degree is a genuine edge, so our job is to make that edge obvious and relevant.

slides.title: Survive the ATS
bullets: One page, single column, plain fonts.
Real text, never an image of text.
No tables or multi-column layouts.
slides.narration: First, survive the machine. Keep your C V to one page, single column, with plain fonts and real selectable text. Never use an image of text, because a parser can't read it. Avoid tables, text boxes, and fancy multi-column layouts, because many parsers scramble them into nonsense and your application quietly gets rejected before any human sees it.

slides.title: A clean CV order
bullets: Name, contact, links up top.
Summary, skills, projects, then experience.
Education and your maths degree last.
slides.narration: Here's an order that works. Name, contact, and your links right at the top. Then a two-line summary, a grouped skills list, and your projects with your strongest one first. After that, your experience, including your support internship, and finally your education and maths degree. The top third of the page is prime real estate, so put your best evidence there.

slides.title: Impact bullets
bullets: Formula: action, tool, metric.
Numbers beat vague verbs.
Even a personal project metric counts.

and shipped it via a FastAPI endpoint.
slides.narration: Now the single biggest upgrade you can make: impact bullets. Weak bullets describe duties, like worked on a model. Strong bullets follow a formula: the action you took, the tools you used, and a measurable result. Numbers can be a model metric, dataset size, latency, or time saved. Even a metric from a personal project beats a vague verb every single time.

slides.title: Frame your background
bullets: Maths degree: probability, linear algebra, proofs.
L1 support: debugging, users, clear comms.
Translate, don't just list.
slides.narration: You might think you lack experience, but you have plenty to translate. Your maths degree gives you probability, linear algebra, and rigorous problem solving, all core to A I. Your level one support internship gave you debugging instincts, real user empathy, and clear communication under pressure. Don't just list these. Frame them as the foundations an A I team actually needs.

slides.title: Tailor keywords honestly
bullets: Mirror the job description's real language.
Lead with the skills that overlap.
Never claim what you can't defend.
slides.code:
matches = [s for s in my_skills
           if s in job_desc.lower()]
print("emphasise:", matches)
slides.narration: Tailor each application. Read the job description and mirror its real language. If it says N L P and PyTorch, use those exact terms wherever they're genuinely true for you. A quick trick is to check which of your skills actually appear in the posting, then lead with those. But never, ever claim a skill you can't defend in an interview.

slides.title: LinkedIn is a search engine
bullets: Headline: target plus concrete skills.
About: maths to AI story, two highlights.
Featured: pin your best repo or demo.
slides.narration: LinkedIn is really a search engine, so three fields do the heavy lifting. Your headline should name your target plus concrete skills, like aspiring M L engineer, Python, N L P. Your About section tells a short story from maths to A I with two project highlights. And your Featured section pins your best repo or demo so a recruiter can click straight through to proof.

slides.title: Make claims verifiable
bullets: Every project maps to a GitHub repo.
Clear README with metrics and how-to-run.
A live demo seals the deal.
slides.code:
git clone https://github.com/you/churn-api
cd churn-api
open README.md
slides.narration: Interviewers probe whatever is on your page, so every claim must be verifiable. Each project should map to a GitHub repo with a clear read-me that explains the metrics and how to run it. A live demo or a notebook seals the deal. Your profile read-me and pinned repos are part of your C V now, so treat them with the same care.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Generic CV sent to every role.
Buzzwords with no evidence.
Hidden white-text keywords — never do this.
slides.narration: Let's flag the mistakes that sink early-career applications. One: sending the same generic C V to every role. Two: buzzwords with nothing behind them, which invite brutal interview questions. And three, please never do this, hiding white-text keywords to trick the A T S. Recruiters spot it and it gets you blacklisted. Honest, specific, and tailored always wins.
